learning_goal: Read the cerebellum as a comparator: it receives a copy of the intended movement and a report of the movement actually happening, computes the difference, and corrects it through the deep nuclei. Attach each of the three functional divisions to what it compares — vestibulocerebellum balance and eye position, spinocerebellum trunk and limb execution, cerebrocerebellum planning and timing — use the climbing fibre as the error signal that makes the system learn, and derive every classical cerebellar sign and bedside test from a comparator that has stopped working rather than memorising a list.

structures.label: The comparator — the one idea the scene is built on
structures.narration: Drawn as a loop with two inputs and one output, because that is what the cerebellum is and everything else in this scene is a consequence of it. Input one is a copy of the command the motor cortex has just issued — an efference copy, arriving by corticopontine and pontocerebellar fibres as mossy fibres. Input two is a report of what the body is actually doing, arriving from muscle spindles, tendon organs, joints and the vestibular apparatus by the spinocerebellar and vestibular routes, also as mossy fibres. The cerebellum holds the two against each other and issues, through the deep nuclei, whatever correction closes the gap. It commands nothing on its own: there is no corticospinal fibre from the cerebellum and a cerebellar lesion causes no weakness. That single fact — a comparator, not a commander — separates cerebellar signs from pyramidal ones at the bedside, and it is why the cerebellum can be destroyed without paralysing anybody.

structures.label: Why it must predict rather than react
structures.narration: The reason a comparator is not enough on its own. Sensory feedback from a moving limb takes long enough to arrive that a system correcting only on feedback oscillates — it is always answering a question about where the limb was, not where it is. So the healthy cerebellum runs the comparison FORWARD: from the efference copy it predicts where the limb will be, and pre-emptively brakes the movement before the target rather than after it. Take that prediction away and the two commonest cerebellar signs fall straight out of the same failure. The limb no longer stops in the right place, which is dysmetria and past-pointing. And it then hunts for the target on delayed feedback, which is the intention tremor that grows as the finger closes on the nose. Both are one deficit — the loss of a prediction — seen at two moments of the same reach.

structures.label: Vestibulocerebellum — balance and the eyes
structures.narration: The oldest division, and the flocculonodular lobe is the whole of it. What it compares is head movement against eye and trunk position, using vestibular input straight from the labyrinth and its own nerve. Its Purkinje cells reach the vestibular nuclei directly, without a deep nucleus of their own — the exception the deep-nuclei scene sets out — and those nuclei act on the eyes through the vestibulo-ocular reflex and on the trunk through the vestibulospinal tract. So its failures are eyes and trunk: nystagmus, and an ataxia of standing and walking with the limbs individually near-normal when tested lying down. The child with a nodular medulloblastoma who cannot sit up but can point accurately is this division alone, and it is the cleanest demonstration in neurology that trunk and limb coordination are separate machinery.

structures.label: Spinocerebellum — the movement while it happens
structures.narration: The vermis and the strip of cortex on either side of it, taken together because they share one input: unconscious proprioception from the body, arriving by the spinocerebellar and cuneocerebellar tracts and carrying a somatotopic map of what every joint is doing right now. This is the division that corrects a movement DURING its execution. The vermis handles the axis — trunk, neck, and the muscles of speech, which is why cerebellar dysarthria with its scanning, syllable-by-syllable rhythm is a midline sign — and outputs through the fastigial nucleus to the vestibular and reticular nuclei. The intermediate zone handles the limbs and outputs through the interposed nucleus to the red nucleus and thalamus. Hypotonia belongs here too: the standing excitation these nuclei supply to the motor system is what sets background tone, so losing it leaves a limb that feels slack and pendular reflexes.

structures.label: Cerebrocerebellum — the movement before it starts
structures.narration: The lateral hemispheres, much the largest division and the one that has expanded with the cerebral cortex it is wired to. Its only substantial input is the cerebral cortex itself, relayed through the pontine nuclei, and its output through the dentate goes back to the motor and premotor cortex by way of the thalamus. It gets no direct sensory input from the limb at all — which is the fact that fixes what it does. It works on the movement before and between muscle contractions: planning the sequence, and above all timing the switch from one muscle group to the next. Dysdiadochokinesia is that timing failing, which is why the test for it is a rapid ALTERNATION rather than a single accurate act. The same timing role is why this division is implicated in non-motor sequencing — the reason a modern account of the cerebellum no longer calls it purely motor.

structures.label: The climbing fibre as an error signal
structures.narration: Why the comparator improves with practice instead of merely correcting. Each Purkinje cell receives thousands of parallel fibres — the granule cells' account of the current context — and exactly ONE climbing fibre from the inferior olive of the opposite side, which wraps it and can fire it at will. Climbing fibres fire rarely, roughly once a second, and they fire when a movement goes wrong. When a climbing fibre discharge coincides with the parallel fibres that were active at the moment of the error, those synapses are weakened — long-term depression — so the same context produces a different output next time. One teacher, thousands of pupils, a lesson delivered only on failure. That is the cellular form of motor learning, and it is what the prism-adaptation experiment measures: a healthy person re-aims within a dozen throws, and a cerebellar patient keeps missing in the same direction, because the error is registered and never used.

structures.label: The signs, all derived from the same failure
structures.narration: The classical list is worth having, but only as an output of the model rather than as a list. Dysmetria and past-pointing: the prediction that should brake the limb is gone. Intention tremor: the limb hunting on delayed feedback near the target. Dysdiadochokinesia: the timing of the switch between antagonists. Dysarthria with scanning speech: the same timing failure applied to the vermis's muscles. Nystagmus: the vestibulocerebellum failing to hold the eyes. Hypotonia and pendular reflexes: the deep nuclei's standing drive to the motor system withdrawn. Truncal and gait ataxia: the midline. Every one of them is on the SAME side as the lesion, for the two-crossings reason the peduncles scene counts out. And none of them is weakness, sensory loss or a resting tremor — the three things that, if present, say the problem is not here.

structures.label: The examination, and what each test is asking
structures.narration: Each bedside test interrogates one division, and knowing which makes the examination an argument instead of a ritual. Finger-nose and heel-shin ask the intermediate zone and the dentate for a predicted stop, so they show dysmetria and intention tremor. Rapid alternating movements ask the lateral hemisphere for timing. Sitting unsupported, standing, and tandem walking ask the vermis and the flocculonodular lobe. Eye movements ask the vestibulocerebellum. One test is routinely misread and is worth stating carefully: Romberg's is NOT a cerebellar test. It asks whether removing vision unmasks a proprioceptive deficit, so it is positive in sensory ataxia and dorsal column disease; a patient with a cerebellar lesion is usually unsteady with the eyes OPEN and does not markedly worsen on closing them. Using Romberg to diagnose cerebellar disease is the commonest error in this examination.

views.title: Two inputs, one output — the comparator
views.narration: Start with the whole machine in one picture, because every sign at the end of this scene is read back off it. A copy of the motor command goes in from the cortex. A report of the actual movement goes in from the muscles, joints and labyrinth. The cerebellum compares them and sends a correction out through its deep nuclei to the systems that are doing the moving. Nothing here is a mesh — this is a drawn circuit, because what the scene teaches is traffic and timing, not shape, and the catalog holds nothing inside the cerebellum in any case. Two consequences to fix before going on. The cerebellum issues no movement of its own, so its lesions never cause weakness. And it works on a copy of the command rather than on the command itself, so it can be removed from the loop and leave the movement crude but present.

views.title: Predicting instead of reacting
views.narration: The step most accounts skip, and it converts two signs from facts to be memorised into things a student can derive. Feedback about a limb arrives too late to steer a fast movement, so a system that only reacted would overshoot and then oscillate. The cerebellum instead predicts the limb's trajectory from the efference copy and brakes it in advance. Remove the prediction and the reach overshoots — dysmetria, past-pointing — and then oscillates as the finger nears the target, which is exactly what an intention tremor is: not a tremor added to the movement, but a corrective loop running too slowly and hunting. Say that out loud once and the difference from a Parkinsonian rest tremor stops needing a rule.

views.title: Three divisions, three jobs, three syndromes
views.narration: The same comparator, applied to three different pairs of things being compared, and the divisions are ordered from the midline outwards exactly as the lobes and nuclei scenes have them. Vestibulocerebellum — flocculonodular lobe — compares head movement with eye and trunk position, and fails as nystagmus and truncal ataxia. Spinocerebellum — vermis and the paravermal strip — compares the command with proprioception arriving now, and fails as dysarthria and midline unsteadiness from the vermis, limb dysmetria and hypotonia from the intermediate zone. Cerebrocerebellum — the lateral hemisphere — has no direct sensory input at all and compares the plan against the cortex's own model, so it fails as bad timing: dysdiadochokinesia, and a movement decomposed into separate steps. Input determines job, and job determines syndrome. That chain is the whole beat.

views.title: Why it gets better with practice
views.narration: A comparator that only corrected would make the same mistake every time. This is the part that learns. Thousands of parallel fibres describe the context to each Purkinje cell; one climbing fibre from the opposite inferior olive reports that the last attempt was wrong. Where the two coincide the parallel fibre synapse is weakened, so the same context yields a different output next time — one teacher, thousands of pupils, and a lesson given only after a failure. That is why a healthy person wearing displacing prisms re-aims within a dozen throws while a cerebellar patient keeps missing the same way. And it is why cerebellar function is better described as calibration than as coordination: the organ's business is keeping the body's model of itself accurate as the body changes.

views.title: From the model to the patient
views.narration: Now derive the examination rather than reciting it. Ask for a predicted stop and you get dysmetria and intention tremor: finger-nose, heel-shin. Ask for timing between antagonists and you get dysdiadochokinesia. Ask the trunk to hold itself and you get midline ataxia; ask the eyes and you get nystagmus. Tone and reflexes show the withdrawn background drive. All of it ipsilateral to the lesion, because two crossings cancel. Two negatives finish the examination and are as diagnostic as the positives: there is no weakness and no sensory loss, and Romberg's test — which asks about proprioception, not coordination — is not the cerebellar sign it is so often taken for. A patient who is steady with the eyes open and falls when they close them has a dorsal column problem, not this one.

gaps: ROUTED TO `diagram`, ITS SECOND PREFERRED MODE, AND THE ROUTING WAS MEASURED THIS RUN. All 934 catalog entries were searched for: cerebell, cerebellum, vermis, tonsil, flocc, nodul, culmen, declive, uvula, dentate, fastigi, emboliform, globose, interposit, peduncle, restiform, brachium, oliv, olivary, pontine, nucle, nucleus, Purkinje, parallel fibre, granule, tract, spinocerebellar, vestibular, red nucleus. The only cerebellar entry is FMA67944 `cerebellum`, undivided; the only `nucle` entries in the whole brain are the two caudate nuclei; there is no olive, no vestibular nucleus, no red nucleus and no tract other than the two optic tracts and the two iliotibial tracts. So the three functional divisions this scene is built on cannot be shown as separate surfaces, and the circuitry it teaches has no surface at all.

THE SUBJECT IS A CIRCUIT, WHICH IS A SECOND AND INDEPENDENT REASON FOR `diagram`, AND A STRONGER ONE THAN THE CATALOG GAP. Even a fully segmented cerebellum would leave all five beats unshown: a comparator, a prediction, an error signal and a bedside sign are none of them shapes. `deferred_modes` keeps `3d_anatomy` on record only because beat 3's three divisions would be worth colouring onto a segmented organ; the other four beats would stay drawn whatever meshes arrive. This is the same judgement the `cerebellar-peduncles` and `deep-cerebellar-nuclei` scenes reached, and it was re-reached here rather than quoted.

STATUS IS `planned`, NOT `ready`, AND NO ARTWORK EXISTS. Promote it when three drawings exist: the comparator loop with both inputs, the deep-nuclei output and the efference copy labelled as such; a three-division panel with each division's input source, output nucleus and failure mode side by side, coloured to match the `cerebellar-lobes` scene's zone colours so a student reads them as the same three strips; and a Purkinje cell with its parallel fibres and its single climbing fibre, with the inhibitory sign drawn on the terminal. The first is load-bearing — beats 1, 2 and 4 are all argument about it.

THIS SCENE CONTAINS NO MODEL IDS AND NO `refs` ON ANY STRUCTURE, following the pattern of the other `diagram` scenes in this course. FMA67944 `cerebellum` and FMA67943 `pons` exist and were deliberately not imported: mixing one real mesh into a drawn circuit would suggest the drawn parts are equally measured. Beat 1 says out loud that nothing here is a mesh, so no beat asks a student to look for something that is not on screen.

NO ANCHORS WERE AUTHORED AND NONE IS POSSIBLE. `tools/derive-landmark.mjs` measures a feature against a parent mesh in `meshes-lite/`; this scene has no parent mesh, and its subjects are functional divisions rather than features on a surface. Nothing was placed by eye.

OVERLAP WITH THE OTHER THREE CEREBELLUM SCENES WAS CHECKED AGAINST THOSE FILES, NOT FROM MEMORY, AND EVERY SHARED FACT IS STATED THE SAME WAY. `cerebellar-lobes` owns the three longitudinal zones and the anterior/posterior/flocculonodular division; this scene uses the identical medial-to-lateral order and the identical functional split (vermis trunk and speech, intermediate zone limb correction during movement, hemisphere planning and timing before movement). `deep-cerebellar-nuclei` owns the four nuclei, the borrowed vestibular nuclei and the inhibitory Purkinje output; this scene names the nuclei only as the output stage of the loop and repeats the FLOCCULONODULAR exception in the same terms — its Purkinje cells leaving the cerebellum directly for the vestibular nuclei, which therefore act as its deep nucleus. (This note originally called that 'the fastigial-to-vestibular exception', which named the wrong structure: the fastigial nucleus DOES project to the vestibular and reticular nuclei, but it does so as an ordinary deep nucleus by the juxtarestiform body, and that is not the exception. Corrected at audit 2026-09-03. Both facts were already stated correctly in the structure cards of both scenes — only this provenance note was wrong.) `cerebellar-peduncles` owns the two crossings; this scene asserts ipsilateral signs and refers the count to that scene rather than restating it, so there is one authority for it in the topic. None of the three is claimed in `covers[]`.

TWO CLAIMS IN THIS SCENE ARE DELIBERATELY LIMITED AND SHOULD NOT BE STRENGTHENED BY A LATER RUN. First, the cerebrocerebellum's non-motor role is named as sequencing and timing and is not extended into specific cognitive or affective syndromes; the evidence is real but the boundaries are disputed, and an exam-facing scene should not adjudicate that. Second, hypotonia is stated as a cerebellar sign without qualification of how prominent it is in chronic human lesions, where it is often slight — if a later run wants that nuance it belongs in this card, not as a contradiction elsewhere.

CURRICULUM VIEWS: `mechanism` is the only required view and all five beats carry it, which is correct rather than lazy — no beat asks the student to look at a surface, and a `location` beat here would duplicate `cerebellar-lobes` beat 1. No other mode is claimed.

OPS THAT REACH OUT OF AN ISOLATED GROUP — reviewed at audit 2026-09-03 and left deliberately in one place, removed in another. `ISOLATE_REGION` ghosts everything outside its group, while `TRACE_STRUCTURE` and `SHOW_RELATIONSHIP` light what they name, so an op naming a structure outside the isolated group is legal but only defensible when the beat's narration actually talks about it. Beat 2's `SHOW_RELATIONSHIP feedforward -> signs` KEPT: that beat's whole argument is that dysmetria and intention tremor fall out of the lost prediction, so the connector is the point. Beat 1's `TRACE_STRUCTURE` path ended on `signs` and was TRIMMED to `loop -> feedforward`: beat 1 names no sign at all, so the trace walked into a ghosted card the student is given no reason to look at. Nothing in the validator distinguishes these two cases — it checks only that the target resolves.

DRAWABILITY: ZERO models referenced, so nothing to deliver and nothing to fetch. The hollowness is entirely at the artwork layer. Note for whoever fetches meshes: a segmented cerebellum would improve one beat of five here, so this scene is a WEAK argument for that fetch — `cerebellar-lobes`, which is already `ready` and 3D, is the strong one.
